texto.en: To say one thing has more or less of a quality, use más or menos + adjective + que: el sofá azul es más barato que el gris, la lámpara es menos cara que la mesa. Que is “than”, and the u is silent: “keh”. To say two things are equal, use tan + adjective + como: esta mesa es tan grande como esa. Tan is short and goes before an adjective. The adjective still agrees with the first thing you mention: la cama es tan cómoda como el sofá. With nouns, use tanto, tanta, tantos or tantas + noun + como, and make tanto agree with the noun: tiene tantas sillas como la otra. With nouns you can also use más and menos: más sillas que, menos dinero que.
Adjectives and tanto agree. Tap each phrase to hear it.

titulo.en: Better, worse, the best, very expensive

texto.en: Four adjectives have special comparatives and never take más: bueno becomes mejor (better) and malo becomes peor (worse). With age, grande becomes mayor (older) and pequeño becomes menor (younger): Daniela es menor que Emma. For size, keep más grande and más pequeño. Mejor and peor are the same for masculine and feminine. To say “the most…”, use the article + más + adjective + de: el microondas más barato de la tienda. With mejor and peor you skip más: el mejor modelo, la peor oferta. Finally, -ísimo means “very”. Drop the final vowel of the adjective and add -ísimo: caro becomes carísimo, barato becomes baratísimo, bueno becomes buenísimo. It agrees like any adjective: carísima, carísimos, carísimas. The stress falls on í: “kah-REE-see-moh”.
These never take más. Tap each phrase to hear it.
Tap each phrase to hear it.

texto.en: To say how clothes or shoes fit you, Spanish uses quedar with me, te or le, plus an adjective: la chaqueta me queda grande means “the jacket is too big for me”. Me queda pequeño means “it's too small”, me queda bien means “it fits well” and me queda mal means “it doesn't fit or suit me”. Notice that English says “too” but Spanish just uses grande or pequeño. Quedar agrees with the clothes, and so does the adjective: la chaqueta me queda grande, but las botas me quedan pequeñas. The pronoun goes before the verb: me queda, te queda, le queda. To ask, use ¿Cómo te queda? with tú and ¿Cómo le queda? with usted: ¿Cómo le quedan las botas? To ask for another size, say ¿Tiene una talla más grande? For shoes, Spanish says el número: ¿Tiene un número más grande?
The verb and the adjective agree with the clothes. Tap each phrase to hear it.
Change the little pronoun to change the person. Tap each phrase to hear it.

explicacion.en: Spanish doesn't allow le or les right before lo, la, los or las. Change le / les to se: se la doy.
The two pronouns stay together before the verb, and the indirect one comes first: se lo, never lo se.
The second pronoun agrees with the thing you send, not with the person: la mesa is feminine, so la.

texto.en: When a sentence has both an indirect object (to whom) and a direct object (what), you can replace both with pronouns. They stay together before the conjugated verb, with the indirect one first: ¿Me la envía? means “Can you send it to me?” (la mesa). Se lo llevamos mañana means “We bring it to you tomorrow” (el sofá). Me, te and nos stay the same, but le and les change to se before lo, la, los or las: Le doy la factura becomes Se la doy. Never say “le la” or “lo se”. This se is not the reflexive se: it replaces le or les and is the same for singular and plural, so context tells you who it is (usted, él, ella, ustedes). The second pronoun agrees with the thing: lo or los for masculine, la or las for feminine. With a verb after puede, the pair can go before the first verb: ¿Me lo puede traer?

After venir, the infinitive of purpose needs a: venía a devolver, venía a cambiar.

titulo.en: Quería and venía a: being polite

texto.en: In a store, quiero (“I want”) can sound too direct. A softer way is quería: Quería preguntar algo, Quería una talla más grande. It looks like the imperfect, but it is about right now, not about the past: it is called the polite imperfect. Use it with usted and with people you don't know. To say why you came to a store, use venía a + infinitive: Venía a cambiar estas botas, Venía a devolver esta lámpara. Remember the a, and the imperfect forms of -er and -ir verbs end in -ía: quería, querías, queríamos, querían; venía, venías, veníamos, venían. The first and third person are identical (yo quería, usted quería), so the subject comes from context. Stress the í: “keh-REE-ah”. Don't use quise for a polite request: it means a finished event.
The imperfect of querer and venir. Tap each form to hear it.

contexto.en: Emma goes back to the shoe store in La Mariscal to exchange the brown boots she bought on sale. She and the salesman use usted with each other.
